title: Dry-Roasted Poha Chivda: A Low-Oil Diwali Snack That Stays Crisp for Weeks
excerpt: Thin poha dry-roasted until crisp, then tossed with nuts and a mustard-seed tempering in just 3 tablespoons of oil — a complete sourced recipe for festive snacking without deep frying.
body:
• Dry-roasted poha chivda delivers the Diwali snack crunch without deep frying: thin poha is roasted on a low flame until crisp, then tossed with nuts roasted in just 3 tablespoons of oil.
  • The recipe card below uses Cook With Di's measured ingredients: 4 cups thin poha, 1/4 cup peanuts, 1/4 cup cashews, 2 tablespoons roasted gram dal, dry coconut, raisins, turmeric, red chilli powder, powdered sugar and amchur.
  • Two storage rules decide whether it stays crisp: cool the chivda completely before sealing it, and fry the chilli and curry leaves until fully dry — Cook With Di says it keeps in an airtight container for up to 2 weeks.
  • Thin poha is non-negotiable for this version; thick poha will not give the same texture.

Every Diwali snack table needs a savoury counterweight to the sweets, and in many Indian homes that job belongs to poha chivda — flattened rice tossed with nuts, spices and curry leaves until it eats, as Cook With Di puts it, like an Indian version of trail mix. The dry-roasted version highlighted by Slurrp for Diwali keeps the method deliberately low-oil: the poha itself is never fried, only roasted until crisp, so the crunch comes from technique rather than a kadhai of oil.

Why Dry Roasting Works

Thin poha is the whole trick. Its flakes are delicate enough to turn crisp over a low flame without absorbing much fat, which is why both recipes consulted insist on thin, not thick, poha. Cook With Di dry-roasts the poha first and sets it aside, then uses a measured 3 tablespoons of oil to roast the peanuts, cashews, roasted gram dal and dry coconut slices for 3–4 minutes, and to bloom mustard seeds, green chillies, curry leaves, hing, turmeric and red chilli powder. The nuts and tempering then coat the roasted poha, finished with salt, powdered sugar and amchur powder.

Wipro Appliances' Maharashtrian version follows the same architecture at a smaller scale — 2 cups thin poha dry-roasted in batches for 5–7 minutes, a tempering built on 2 tablespoons of oil, and storage in an airtight jar — and notes the roasted, rather than deep-fried, method makes the snack lighter and easier to digest. The agreement between the two recipes is the useful signal for a first-time maker: roast low, stir gently, do not let the flakes brown, and season while the mixture is warm so the spices cling.

The Recipe

The card below reproduces Cook With Di's ingredients and method exactly, because a recipe card is only useful if its quantities were tested by its source. Dry roast 4 cups of thin poha on a low flame until crisp and set it aside. Heat the oil, roast the peanuts until crisp, add cashew, roasted gram dal and dry coconut slices for 3–4 minutes, then the raisins until they puff; set the nuts aside. Crackle the mustard seeds in the same pan, sauté the green chillies and curry leaves until crisp and dry, add hing, turmeric, red chilli powder and the roasted nuts, then fold everything through the poha with salt, powdered sugar and amchur. That is the complete method — no soaking, no frying of the base, no special equipment beyond a wide pan.

Storage and Serving for the Diaspora Kitchen

Chivda is made for making ahead, which suits diaspora Diwali planning: a batch cooked on a weekend can serve guests, fill gift jars and stock the tea-time tin. Two rules protect the texture. Cool the mixture completely before storing it, Cook With Di advises, and make sure the chilli and curry leaves are fried crisp and dry — any moisture left in them turns stored chivda soggy. Stored airtight, Cook With Di says it keeps for up to 2 weeks; Wipro's version, stored cool and dry in an airtight jar, is given 3–4 weeks. Use the shorter, two-week window if your kitchen is humid.

Customise within the frame the sources allow: Cook With Di notes you can add any nuts of your choice. Serve it beside the mithai, pack it in decorative jars as a homemade gift, or — the use every maker recognises — keep a tin within reach of the kettle. It is the Diwali snack that disappears handful by handful while the bigger cooking is still under way.

author: Diaspora Desk

steps: Add thin poha in a wide pan. Dry roast on low flame till it is crisp. Keep it aside.
In the same pan heat oil. Add peanuts and roast till crisp.
Add cashew, roasted gram dal, dry coconut slices and roast for 3-4 minutes.
Then add raisin and roast till the raisins puff up. Keep the nuts aside.
In the same pan add mustard seeds and let it crackle.
Add green chili, curry leaves and saute till crisp and dry. Then add hing, turmeric, red chili powder, roasted nuts and mix well.
Now add nuts mixture to roasted poha along with salt, powdered sugar, aamchur powder and mix everything well.
Cool completely before storing; store in an airtight container for up to 2 weeks.
